idiom_name: abstract record Either<TLeft, TRight> with nested sealed Left/Right
implementation_notes: The BCL has no Either, so the type is written by hand as a closed hierarchy: one abstract record Either<TLeft, TRight> with two nested sealed records, consumed by a switch expression over the two cases (records bring value equality and property patterns destructure them). The compiler warns when a switch expression can be proven non-exhaustive, but it cannot prove exhaustiveness for arbitrary pattern combinations, so the final discard arm should throw UnreachableException instead of returning a default - that way a forgotten case fails loudly. LanguageExt supplies Either<L, R> among its monads when the project already programmes C# in that style.
pitfalls: A switch expression over a class hierarchy is not exhaustiveness-checked the way a Rust match or a Java sealed switch is: the discard arm compiles silently, so it must throw.

Records are reference types with value equality, and the nested Left/Right types are distinct per type argument, so generic helpers need their own type parameters - an Either<string, int> is not an Either<object, object>.
Mixing the hand-written Either with LanguageExt's Either in one codebase produces two incompatible types that cannot be passed to the same helper; pick one for the whole project.

variants.name: LanguageExt Either<L, R>
variants.idiom_name: LanguageExt.Core Either<L, R> with Match and Prelude helpers
variants.implementation_notes: LanguageExt documents Either<L, R> among its monads, next to Option<A>, the state-handling monads and the monad-transformers (types with a T suffix), and the Prelude supplies the constructor and combinator functions for the whole library. Choose it when the codebase already programmes C# in that style, so that Either interoperates with Option, Try and the rest of the prelude instead of standing beside them; the cost is a substantial dependency and a set of conventions the whole team has to follow.
pitfalls: The constructors and combinators come from LanguageExt.Prelude (using static): without it the helpers are unavailable and the type is awkward to build, so the import is part of the convention.

Adopting the library is a codebase-wide decision: its Either does not interoperate with a hand-written Either or with nullable-reference-typed BCL idioms, and mixing the two error contracts in one API forces callers to learn both.
